summary: OAuth App credentials in about 1 minute with no review step; organizations that restrict third-party apps may still need an owner to approve your app before you can access their data.

time.setup_notes: Registration itself took about 30 seconds in a supervised test (Supervised browser agent (Claude in Chrome), 2026-10-29); about 1 minute including reading the form. This does not include writing the OAuth flow in your app.

approval_wait.label: None
approval_wait.notes: The app was live the moment it was registered; there is no review step for the developer's own app (Supervised browser agent (Claude in Chrome), 2026-10-29). Organization owners can still gate access to org data separately.

prerequisites.notes: Register under a personal account or an organization you own.
Full URL to your app's website.
At least one is required; the form takes a list of up to 10, with optional wildcard matching. http://localhost URLs are accepted.
Only for orgs that restrict third-party app access and only to read their private data.

steps.title: Open the OAuth App registration form
steps.detail: Settings > Developer settings > OAuth Apps > New OAuth App (or the organization's equivalent under its settings).

steps.title: Enter app details
steps.detail: Provide the application name, the homepage URL and at least one redirect URI (add more to the list if you need them). Only use information you consider public. Device Flow is optional and off by default. Click Register application; the app is live immediately.

steps.title: Generate and store the client secret
steps.detail: Registration does not create a secret. On the new app settings page, copy the Client ID, click "Generate a new client secret", and keep both in environment variables, never in client-side code.

steps.title: Decide on expiring user tokens
steps.detail: 'Expire user access tokens' is checked by default. Leave it on and implement refresh tokens unless your app cannot yet handle short-lived tokens.

steps.title: Implement the authorization code flow
steps.detail: Redirect users to GitHub's authorize URL, exchange the returned code for a token server-side, and request the minimum scopes.

steps.title: Get organization approval if required
steps.detail: If a user's organization restricts third-party apps, an owner must approve your app before it can access org data.

scopes.notes: Needed when the primary email is private.
Prefer over repo when private access is unnecessary.

scopes.purpose: Full access to public and private repositories.
scopes.notes: Very broad; org owners are more likely to deny it. A GitHub App offers finer permissions.

blockers.issue: Users in organizations with OAuth app access restrictions cannot grant your app access to org data until an org owner approves it.
blockers.how_to_resolve: Ask the organization owner to approve the app under the organization's Settings → Third-party application access.
blockers.verified_with: Supervised browser agent (Claude in Chrome), 2026-10-29. The restricted policy ("Access restricted": only approved apps can access org data) was observed on a test org; a member being blocked was not exercised.

blockers.issue: You need fine-grained or per-repository permissions.
blockers.how_to_resolve: Use a GitHub App instead of an OAuth App.

agent_can_do: Suggest app name, homepage and callback URLs
Recommend minimum scopes for the use case
Write the authorization code flow and token refresh code
Draft the request to an org owner for approval
developer_must_do: Register the OAuth App while signed in to GitHub
Generate and securely store the client secret
Get organization owner approval where required

claims_evidence.claim: Registering an OAuth App takes an application name, a homepage URL and at least one redirect URI; the app is live as soon as it is registered, with no review or approval step. The only approval-related option on the form is an optional "List this application in the Marketplace" button.
Redirect URIs are a list of up to 10 entries, with an optional "Allow wildcard matching" checkbox, rather than a single callback URL field.
'Expire user access tokens' is checked by default on a new OAuth App.
No client secret is created at registration; the app settings page has a "Generate a new client secret" button, so the secret is generated on demand.
http://localhost redirect URIs are accepted at registration (one with a port, and one with a port and a path, were both accepted with no warning).
No scopes are chosen when registering an OAuth App; there is no scope field, and the app requests scopes at login time.
Registration took about 30 seconds from opening the form to the "Application created successfully" banner, so setup takes about 1 minute.
An organization whose Third-party application access policy is "Access restricted" only lets approved apps access org data.
A user or organization can own up to 100 OAuth apps.
No scope triggers a GitHub review; scope breadth only affects whether org owners approve.

composio_managed_auth.notes: Composio maintains a managed OAuth app for GitHub, so you can start without registering your own.
composio_managed_auth.supporting_quote: Composio registers and maintains OAuth apps for popular toolkits such as GitHub, Gmail, and Slack.

meta.verification_method: Supervised browser agent (Claude in Chrome) registered a real OAuth App on a test account on 2026-10-29, inspected the form and settings pages, then deleted the app.

notes.title: OAuth App vs GitHub App
notes.text: Permissions: a GitHub App has fine-grained permissions (repository, organization, account, enterprise) and event subscriptions; an OAuth App requests scopes at login. Webhooks: a GitHub App has a webhook (Active toggle, URL, secret); an OAuth App has none. Install flow: a GitHub App is installed on accounts, with an optional Setup URL, 'Redirect on update' and 'Request user authorization (OAuth) during installation', and asks whether it can be installed 'Only on this account' or 'Any account'; an OAuth App has no such choice. Both share redirect URIs, device flow and token-expiry options.
